summary: Introductory partner discovery between Redwood (AE+SE) and Copper Arc Systems to evaluate hybrid GPU onramp integration. Key topics: integration patterns (hosted vs dedicated vs private), performance baselines, scheduling a benchmark/pilot on partner GPUs, security/compliance requirements, and commercial framing for a pilot. Agreed next steps include sharing pilot pricing, model lists, and scheduling a 1-week performance window.
topics: Partner onramp patterns: direct routing vs gateway proxy
Performance profiling and hardware equivalence (A100/GB200 mapping)
Commercial pilot: credits, capacity, success criteria
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-24
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Maya Patel, Alex Chen, Jordan Lee
Attendees (Customer): Ravi Menon, Leah Torres, Ben Cohen, Samira Ortiz

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Ravi Menon: Hey Maya, Ravi here.
[00:09] Leah Torres: Leah, CTO.
[00:11] Ben Cohen: Ben, infra.
[00:13] Samira Ortiz: Samira, security.
[00:15] Alex Chen: Alex, SE at Redwood.
[00:17] Jordan Lee: Jordan, solutions eng.

[01:00] Maya Patel: Cool, the agenda we sent was roughly partner integration patterns, perf expectations, security/compliance, and commercial pilot framing. Feel free to correct or add.
[01:12] Leah Torres: That looks good. We're mainly trying to understand how Redwood could route workloads to our GPU pool and what the integration overhead looks like. Also want clarity on what runs in Copper Arc vs what stays in Redwood control plane.

[02:10] Alex Chen: High level: Redwood supports three modes — Hosted API, Dedicated (reserved capacity on provider), and Private (VPC/on-prem). For a partner onramp we typically see a gateway/proxy pattern where requests can be routed to a partner's infra as a model variant. That keep's our control plane for billing/observability but executes inference on partner GPUs.
[02:36] Ben Cohen: So the exec path — is the KV cache or batching managed by Redwood runtime or do we need to implement anything on our side?
[02:45] Alex Chen: Good question. Batch and KV cache live in the runtime that runs where the model runs. If you run our runtime on Copper Arc GPUs (like a sidecar/container), it handles batching and prefix/KV caching; the only integration point is a lightweight routing proxy and SNI/TLS for auth. We do have a fallback mode where Redwood hosts a lightweight fast-path for short requests if partner capacity is saturated.

[03:40] Ravi Menon: Right. Our business model is to supply GPU capacity as an onramp for SaaS customers; we want to meter utilization and offer predictable latency SLAs. What's Redwood's SLA expectations per model?
[03:52] Jordan Lee: We typically shape SLAs at Dedicated level. For 99th percentile latency SLOs we combine kernel selection, batching, and routing policies. We can expose per-token latency goals — e.g., targeting 300–500ms p50 for 2k token sequences with an A100-class GPU. But that depends on model, quantization, and batch sizes.

[04:30] Leah Torres: A couple things on our side: our GPU fleet is heterogeneous — mixture of 80GB A100-equivalent nodes and some newer Hopper/GB200 types. We need mapping guidance.
[04:42] Alex Chen: Totally. We do model-to-hardware profiling during onboarding. We can produce a mapping doc that recommends which model variants/quantization profile to run on each GPU type. Quick caveat: we may do different kernel selection for GB200 vs A100; throughput numbers differ. We'll run a short profiling job.

[06:05] Ben Cohen: How intrusive is Redwood's runtime? Can it be containerized or do you expect a VM image?
[06:12] Jordan Lee: Containerized is fine; most partners run a containerized agent. We provide Helm charts for K8s or a simple daemonset for clusters. If you prefer an AMI-like image we can produce that as well.

[07:00] Samira Ortiz: Security — we need to know about data plane encryption, customer-managed KMS, and audit logs. We can't allow unencrypted model cache on disk in our environment.
[07:12] Alex Chen: Understood. Our runtime supports in-transit TLS and optional disk encryption. For KMS, we have integrations for customer-managed keys (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HSM) so the runtime encrypts caches. Also we can send audit logs to your SIEM via syslog or S3 sink. We'll share SOC2 artifacts.

[08:35] Leah Torres: Any gotchas around multi-tenancy? We don't want noisy neighbors affecting other customers.
[08:41] Jordan Lee: We recommend namespace-level isolation and GPU cgroups or MIG where possible. We also support per-route QoS shaping at the proxy-level; Dedicated pools can be dedicated to a particular customer to avoid noisy neighbor issues.

[10:05] Maya Patel: Commercially, what's most valuable — pilot with 1–2 enterprise customers or a marketplace listing?
[10:12] Ravi Menon: Pilot first. Prove reliability and latency. Then marketplace listing and revenue share.

[11:00] Alex Chen: For the pilot we suggest a 1-week benchmark window where Redwood will route test traffic to Copper Arc staging, collect token-level latency, tail latency, and throughput. We'll need a model list and traffic patterns.
[11:20] Ben Cohen: We'll provide models — 2 conv models and 1 LLM for embeddings/search. Expect sequences ~256 tokens average, 95th pct around 1,200 tokens for long form. QPS baseline unknown — probably 20–50 qps for initial pilot.

[12:45] Maya Patel: Great. On pricing we can do pilot credits and then a Reserved Dedicated pricing or revenue share for marketplace. I'll share a spreadsheet with the unit economics and also a Hosted vs Dedicated comparison.
[13:05] Ravi Menon: What's the routing latency added by Redwood proxy — like extra hop? We're sensitive to end-to-end p95.
[13:15] Jordan Lee: Minimal — if the runtime is colocated in your network and we use private peering, added latency is usually in the single-digit ms. Bigger sources of tail are batching and kernel warmup. We'll instrument and show you the breakdown per-token.

[14:30] Samira Ortiz: Regarding compliance, we run SOC2 Type II. We will need Redwood's SOC2 and any encryption attestations before we go live. Also contractually we need data residency language for EU customers.
[14:45] Maya Patel: We'll share SOC2 and our security pack. We have enterprise contracts that include data residency and subprocessor lists.

[16:20] Leah Torres: Integration ownership — who maintains runtime updates? If Redwood releases a runtime patch, do we coordinate rolling updates or do you push them?
[16:30] Alex Chen: Typically partner-run clusters manage the runtime; Redwood will provide release notes and an operator image. For critical patches we can coordinate a forced upgrade window; otherwise partner ops control upgrades.

[17:50] Ben Cohen: On the tech stack: are there any special kernel requirements? For example, cuBLAS vs Cutlass or custom kernels for GB200?
[18:00] Jordan Lee: We have a kernel selector that chooses optimized kernels. For GB200 we sometimes use vendor-provided fused attention kernels. We'll include a short runbook of fallbacks. For quantized models we may use Triton/flash-attn variants.

[19:45] Ravi Menon: Are there telemetry hooks we can forward to our console? We want to charge customers and show usage.
[19:54] Alex Chen: Yes — we expose a webhook-based usage export and metrics endpoint. For billing we'd export token counts, model id, and request metadata. We can also forward traces to your trace collector.

[21:30] Leah Torres: Let's talk about success criteria for the pilot. For us, it's 95th percentile latency under X ms and less than Y% error rate. We also want predictable cost per 1k tokens.
[21:45] Maya Patel: Makes sense. Typical pilot success criteria we propose: 1) baseline throughput and p95 latency within 20% of Redwood internal numbers for same model, 2) <1% error rate, 3) integration with billing/usage export working end-to-end.

[23:00] Ben Cohen: On observed token lengths — we'll send a histogram. Our longer sequences cause memory pressure so we'd appreciate recommendations for KV caching and prefix reuse.
[23:12] Jordan Lee: We'll analyze your token histogram and recommend cache TTLs and shard sizes. For long tails we propose a hybrid route: short requests served with aggressive batching and long ones pinned to lower-concurrency instances to avoid OOMs.

[25:10] Alex Chen: A quick note on fallbacks — we can set policies to move traffic to Redwood-hosted smaller quantized variants if partner capacity is saturated. That keeps app availability but may slightly change latency/quality.
[25:28] Ravi Menon: That tradeoff is acceptable for many customers, but we want transparency in the Console when that happens.
[25:35] Maya Patel: Console will show route-level fallbacks, percentage of requests, and cost delta.

[27:40] Samira Ortiz: Any PII concerns in model cache? We need to ensure data retention policies and purge windows.
[27:48] Alex Chen: We support configurable retention and immediate purge APIs; runtime exposes purge-by-request-id. We'll add that to the security doc.

[30:00] Maya Patel: Ok let's outline the pilot steps: 1) Copper Arc provides model list + traffic profile, 2) Redwood shares pilot pricing + baseline plan, 3) set up staging cluster and run a 7-day benchmark, 4) review results and decide on marketplace vs Dedicated.
[30:20] Leah Torres: Agreed. Timelines? We want to start benchmarks in the next two weeks if possible.
[30:28] Maya Patel: We'll aim to start staging by 2026-04-06. Sound OK?
[30:35] Ben Cohen: That works but we need internal sign-off on capacity allocation; I'll confirm by 2026-03-26.

[32:10] Jordan Lee: For the benchmarking we recommend three workloads: 1) low-latency chat, 2) batched embeddings, 3) long-form generation. We'll run load at target QPS and stepped increases to find saturation.
[32:30] Alex Chen: We'll also capture kernel-level metrics and KV cache hit rate so we can tune batch sizes.

[34:40] Ravi Menon: On commercial side, revenue sharing for marketplace — what's Redwood's typical split?
[34:50] Maya Patel: Typical marketplace resale varies; for pilot we usually focus on throughput credits and a simple revenue share proposal for later — we'll include sample options in the spreadsheet.

[36:12] Leah Torres: One more technical — support for Model quantization on your side? Can Redwood handle INT8/4-bit flows?
[36:20] Jordan Lee: Yes we support quantized runtimes and can recommend quantization profiles per model. Quality regressions can be validated via eval prompts; Redwood Optimize can help detect regressions.

[38:05] Ben Cohen: Are there any legal items we should prepare — subprocessor list, DPA?
[38:12] Maya Patel: We'll send our DPA and subprocessor list. For marketplace we'll need a simple reseller agreement; legal can draft after the pilot.

[40:10] Samira Ortiz: We may require a short security call with your security team — go over config, key management, and network peering.
[40:18] Maya Patel: Absolutely — we'll set that up.

[42:30] Alex Chen: Quick note — we occasionally see perf surprises when partners have heavy noisy neighbor GC or virtualization overhead. We'll do a short pre-run to validate perf without customer traffic.

[44:00] Leah Torres: If we wanted to run initial tests ourselves and forward synthetic traffic, can you provide a test harness?
[44:08] Jordan Lee: Yes, we'll provide a JMeter-like harness and a small client that mimics Redwood tokenization and request pacing so the runtime sees realistic patterns.

[46:30] Ravi Menon: Ok — sounds like we have a plan. Anything else from Redwood?
[46:36] Maya Patel: I'll follow up with the pilot doc, pricing, and SOC2 pack. Alex will coordinate the perf plan. Jordan will provide the operator helm chart.

[48:05] Ben Cohen: We'll provide the model list and histogram by Thursday. Samira will send compliance contacts.

[50:00] Maya Patel: Recap — pilot start target 2026-04-06, action items captured. Any blockers?
[50:08] Leah Torres: No blockers. Need legal review but it's routine.

[52:30] Ravi Menon: One small ask — can Redwood annotate latency with model variant and kernel selection in the metrics so we can correlate regressions?
[52:40] Alex Chen: Yes metrics include model_id, variant, kernel, and instance_id.

[54:10] Samira Ortiz: Please include an encrypted channel for credential exchange; we prefer an SFTP drop or KMS-wrapped secret.
[54:18] Jordan Lee: We'll support KMS-wrapped secrets and a secure drop.

[56:00] Maya Patel: Cool. If no other items, we'll close. Thanks everyone.
[56:05] Leah Torres: Thanks all.
[56:12] Ben Cohen: Thanks.
[56:15] Ravi Menon: Thanks Maya and team.
[56:18] Maya Patel: One more note — shared doc links: pilot-pricing.xlsx (will attach), soc2-pack.zip (will attach), helm-chart repo link (will send).
[56:40] Alex Chen: Expect perf baseline deliverable after we receive model artifacts.
[57:00] (call ends)
